nameStory: Hoy's Jumping Spider carries the name of Dr. Phil Hoy, likely an arachnologist who contributed to our understanding of these nimble hunters. Like many scientific names that honor researchers, this spider's moniker connects us to the human story of discovery and the dedicated scientists who first studied these remarkable little predators.
description: Hoy's Jumping Spider is a small, compact hunter that belongs to the most athletic family of spiders. These spiders don't build webs to catch prey - instead, they leap impressive distances to pounce on unsuspecting insects. With their characteristically large front eyes and fuzzy bodies, they're often considered the most charismatic of all spiders. They're quite small, typically measuring less than half an inch in body length.

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Four large eyes arranged in a square pattern on the face, with the front pair notably bigger and more prominent, giving them an almost mammal-like expression that seems to track your movements

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, stocky build with a somewhat flattened appearance and fuzzy texture that feels like velvet when gently touched

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves in quick, jerky motions with sudden stops, often turning to face you directly when approached, and capable of impressive leaps several times their body length

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: No web for catching prey, but may create small silk retreats under bark or stones that feel like tiny sleeping bags

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small spider with body length typically around a quarter to half inch, about the size of a large peppercorn

habitat: Look for Hoy's Jumping Spider in sunny, open areas where they can hunt effectively - meadows, forest edges, and gardens are prime spots. They're often found on flowers, fence posts, or tree bark where they can easily spot flying insects. These spiders prefer areas with good visibility and plenty of insect activity to support their active hunting lifestyle.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, often seen sunbathing on south-facing surfaces in the morning to warm up their muscles for hunting.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible, actively hunting and mating, with males performing elaborate courtship dances with their legs and colorful body parts.
seasonality.fall: Females create silk egg sacs in protected locations while adults prepare for winter by seeking shelter under bark or in rock crevices.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically don't survive the cold, but eggs overwinter in protected silk sacs, waiting for spring warmth to hatch into tiny spiderlings.

funFact: Jumping spiders have better color vision than humans, seeing into the ultraviolet spectrum, which means the flowers and insects they hunt appear in brilliant colors we can't even imagine - like having built-in psychedelic sunglasses!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small jumping spiders, but remember that all jumping spiders share those distinctive large front eyes and compact, fuzzy bodies. If it's staring back at you with big eyes and can leap impressive distances, you've found a jumper - the exact species often requires close examination of markings and size.
compareHints: Since Hoy's Jumping Spider is the only Evarcha species commonly found in New England, compare it to other jumping spiders like the Bold Jumping Spider, which is notably larger and more robust. Hoy's tends to be smaller and more delicate in build than the chunky Bold Jumper, though both share the family's characteristic large eyes and hunting behavior.
